analysis.one_liner: Cuts corporate taxes, restricts federal regulation and carbon rules, limits lawsuits, and expands offshore and pipeline fossil fuel development.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any of the eight committees it was referred to, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced near the end of the 113th Congress, bundled together several Republican priorities: cutting the corporate tax rate from 35% to 25%, making business tax breaks permanent, requiring Congress to approve major federal regulations before they take effect, blocking the EPA's carbon rules for power plants, expanding offshore oil and gas drilling and pipeline permitting, and making it easier to sanction attorneys who file lawsuits. It was referred to eight House committees but none of them ever acted on it, so it never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, especially manufacturers and energy producers: they would pay a 25% corporate tax rate instead of 35%, keep permanent expensing and research tax breaks, face fewer environmental and permitting constraints (including on Keystone XL, natural gas pipelines, fracking, and offshore drilling), and face fewer lawsuits under tightened Rule 11 sanctions and patent pleading rules. Fossil fuel interests gain access to offshore lease sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California, and 37.5% of new federal leasing revenues would go to nearby coastal states.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, manufacturers, and fossil fuel companies

how_it_helps.text: It cuts the corporate income tax rate to 25% and makes permanent the research credit, bonus depreciation, and expanded small-business expensing, reducing taxes on manufacturers and other corporations.

It requires Congress to approve major federal regulations before they take effect, and specifically bars the EPA from enforcing greenhouse gas standards for new and existing fossil-fuel power plants under conditions it sets.

It expands fossil fuel access: fast-tracking the Keystone XL pipeline, requiring 12-month approval deadlines for natural gas pipeline permits, barring federal fracking regulation in states that have their own rules, and mandating offshore oil and gas lease sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California.

It makes courts impose mandatory sanctions in Rule 11 litigation, tightens pleading standards in patent cases, and requires quarterly asbestos-claim reporting in bankruptcy, all of which reduce litigation exposure for companies.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the cost of the tax cuts, which the bill explicitly exempts from pay-as-you-go scorecards (Sec. 1007). Over time, the revenue gap shifts to future taxpayers or spending cuts. Consumers and communities near coal plants and new drilling bear increased pollution and climate risk from weakened EPA authority and expanded fossil fuel development. People injured by products or pollution face higher barriers to suing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal treasury, and people near new fossil fuel development

drawbacks.text: Cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 25% and making business tax breaks permanent would reduce federal revenue, and the bill exempts these effects from PAYGO scorecards, meaning no offsetting savings are required.

The bill would block EPA greenhouse gas standards for power plants unless technology is already proven at existing units, bar use of the social cost of carbon in regulatory analysis, and nullify existing proposed carbon rules — removing constraints on utility emissions that affect public health and climate.

Mandatory sanctions under Rule 11 and removal of the 21-day safe harbor would make it riskier for attorneys to file suit, including legitimate claims, which could reduce access to the courts for injured consumers and workers.

Requiring Congress to affirmatively approve every major federal rule before it takes effect would routinely leave costly public-health, safety, and environmental rules unenforced when Congress fails to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles some broadly popular ideas (a permanent R&D credit, faster permitting) with large corporate tax cuts, a congressional veto over federal regulations, blocking climate rules, and expanded fossil fuel leasing. The drawbacks are serious: the tax cuts were unpaid and tilted toward profitable corporations, the regulatory provisions would weaken the main tools for protecting air quality and addressing climate change, and the tort changes would make it harder to sue over injuries. Congress never weighed any of this; the bill was referred to eight committees and multiple subcommittees and died there.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees and several subcommittees after introduction, but none of them ever took it up, so it never reached the House floor and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 31, 2014, the bill was referred to eight House committees, with no markup or floor action ever scheduled.
Subcommittee referrals in August and September 2014 were the last recorded actions before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
It carried 19 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never attracted Democratic support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing potential EPA carbon regulations, corporate tax increases, litigation, and permitting delays — none of the bill's provisions took effect, so existing tax rates, EPA authority, and court rules continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: no one gained; regulation and taxes unchanged

for.name: 19 House Republican cosponsors (including Reps. Hensarling, Jordan, DeSantis, and Schweikert)

against.name: House Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and other committee chairs
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over referred provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled any markup or action on the bill after its referral to eight committees and multiple subcommittees.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: A 25% corporate rate, permanent R&D credit, bonus depreciation, and expensing, plus limits on litigation and regulatory approval requirements, directly cut costs for large companies.
Keystone fast-tracking, pipeline permitting deadlines, state-level fracking control, and mandatory offshore lease sales open new acreage and reduce federal oversight.

industries.industry: Coal-burning electric utilities and coal producers
industries.note: The bill nullifies EPA carbon rules for power plants and sets near-impossible conditions for new standards, protecting coal-fired generation from regulation.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline and electric transmission developers
industries.note: Faster FERC permitting benefits pipeline builders, but new cross-border certificates add a process; overall a net gain for energy infrastructure firms.

industries.industry: Trial-bar opponents / corporate defendants (insurers and corporate litigants)
industries.note: Mandatory sanctions and asbestos-claim transparency reduce litigation costs borne by companies facing injury and patent suits.
Mandatory Rule 11 sanctions without a safe harbor and quarterly asbestos reporting make injury litigation riskier and claims more visible to companies seeking to contest them.
